newsitem.title: USA: U.N. says Iraq aid plan approval seen next week.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says Iraq aid plan approval seen next week.

text.p: Iraq's aid distribution plan, made necessary for resuming oil exports under the $2-billion "oil-for-food" accord, is expected to gain U.N. approval early next week, U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said Thursday.
Technical glitches with a computer disc sent from Baghdad earlier in the week to New York, along with the bulk of the 678-page annex to the main aid plan, extended the review.
"It is a meticulous review, it is alot of pages, it is going to take an extra day," Eckhard said. "One of the diskettes we have had a virus and we had to get an extra diskette from Baghdad."
In addition, the U.N. secretariat was awaiting a routine review by U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) inspectors.
Eckhard said the U.N. believed it had settled the issue of Iraq providing distribution of food and medicines for "vulnerable groups" in the northern, Kurdish-majority sections of the country.
"It is settled from our point of view. We asked Iraq for certain assurances on that subject and we received them in writing," Eckhard said.
The problem arose after Baghdad did not earmark funds in the new plan for the sick, elderly or children, considered particularly in need of food or medicine.
Earlier this week, a U.N. humanitarian aid official said the size of the annexes and the fact only one copy was sent to New York headquarters this past Monday, slowed the review.
"They (the aid plan annexes) had to be copied for many teams, and this took a long time," said the U.N. source.
Iraq has demanded that the aid plan, which sets conditions and logistics for the humanitarian half of the $2 billion "oil-for-food" accord, be approved before oil sales resume.

Iraq's stance has effectively squelched the start for second round oil sales under the accord, despite the fact the U.N. Security Council approved a 180-day extension from June 8, U.N. officials said.
At issue is the "oil-for-food" accord, a U.N.-sponsored exception to broad sanctions slapped on Baghdad after Iraqi troops invaded Kuwait in August, 1990.
Iraq is permitted to sell $2 billion worth of crude oil, plus another $140 million for pipeline fees to Turkey, over a period of six months, running from June 8 to December 4.
